timeline.heading: A gentler shift, one day at a time
timeline.wellness: This is general wellness information, not medical advice or a diagnosis. Keep your usual sleep needs and personal health in mind.

guidance.sleepShift: Aim to sleep around {bedtime} and wake around {wakeTime}, shifting your usual schedule {movement} gradually.
guidance.sleepOpportunity: Aim for a sleep opportunity around {bedtime}–{wakeTime} local time while protecting your usual sleep duration.
guidance.lightMinimal: Spend time outdoors during local daytime and keep your usual sleep routine.
guidance.lightUncertain: Exact light timing is uncertain for this timezone change. Favor ordinary daytime outdoor light, dim light before sleep, and avoid using bright-light devices to force a shift.
guidance.lightPreflightEast: After waking, get ordinary outdoor light when practical; dim bright indoor light before your earlier bedtime.
guidance.lightPreflightWest: Keep ordinary evening light while shifting later; make your sleep environment dark at bedtime.
guidance.lightDestination: Get outdoor light during destination daytime when practical and keep light low as you approach planned sleep. Exact biological timing cannot be measured from these inputs.
guidance.caffeine: If you choose caffeine, use it earlier in your waking period; avoid it from {cutoff} onward (8 hours before planned sleep).
guidance.tripUncertain: This trip crosses a date-line-sized offset change, so a simple east/west adaptation direction could be misleading.
guidance.tripMinimal: The timezone difference is small, so a major sleep shift may not be useful.
guidance.tripDirectional: Circadian timing varies between people; these gradual schedule changes are estimates, not a measurement of your body clock.
guidance.preparationMinimal: Keep your usual sleep schedule today; the timezone difference is small and does not call for a 30-minute shift.
guidance.preparationShift: Move the schedule by about 30 minutes {movement} today. Keep your normal sleep opportunity; do not cut sleep short to follow the plan.
guidance.arrival: {explanation} Follow destination-local clock times and use these suggestions only where they fit safely with the flight and your sleep needs.
guidance.postArrival: {explanation} A consistent local sleep and wake schedule supports adjustment.
guidance.limitedPreparation: Only {count} preflight preparation day is available; the plan does not make up missed days with larger shifts.
guidance.limitedPreparationPlural: Only {count} preflight preparation days are available; the plan does not make up missed days with larger shifts.
guidance.lightLimitation: Precise light seek/avoid times are not estimated for this timezone change because biological circadian phase is unknown.
guidance.minimalLimitation: The estimated timezone difference is under one hour; focus on adequate sleep and local routine rather than a major shift.

science.title: The science of timezone adaptation — VoyageClock
science.description: Learn how circadian rhythms, light, sleep schedules, and caffeine relate to jet lag.
science.eyebrow: A LITTLE SCIENCE, A LOT OF CONTEXT
science.headline:
Your body clock
runs on
science.intro: Jet lag is the mismatch between your internal rhythms and local time after crossing time zones. Light is a powerful cue for the body clock—but timing is the important part.
science.lightTitle: Light can shift your clock in either direction
science.lightOne: Light exposure at different points in the circadian cycle can move the clock earlier or later. The effect depends on biological timing, not just what the clock on the wall says. Without measuring your circadian phase, a generic “get morning light” instruction can be too simplistic—particularly after a large timezone change.
science.lightTwo: That’s why VoyageClock keeps light advice practical and qualified. For larger or ambiguous shifts, it explains the uncertainty instead of claiming to know the perfect exposure window.
science.sleepTitle: Protect sleep while making gradual changes
science.sleepOne: Before travel, modest adjustments to bedtime and wake time may make the transition feel more manageable. Research has tested advancing schedules combined with timed bright light before eastward travel, but the studied protocol and participants are not identical to every traveler.
science.sleepTwo: VoyageClock starts with small schedule steps and preserves your usual sleep opportunity. It does not make up for missed preparation days by asking you to abruptly shift or sleep less.
science.caffeineTitle: Caffeine can trade alertness for sleep
science.caffeineOne: Caffeine can help with alertness, but its effects can linger and interfere with sleep. A practical plan can suggest avoiding it in the hours before intended bedtime; individual sensitivity and caffeine metabolism vary.
science.caffeineTwo: VoyageClock’s eight-hour cutoff is a conservative sleep-planning rule based on general sleep guidance, not a personalized measurement of how your body processes caffeine.
science.limitationsTitle: What this plan can—and can’t—tell you
science.limitationOne: It uses the times and timezone information you provide to create a simple schedule.
science.limitationTwo: It does not measure your circadian phase, predict exactly when jet lag symptoms will end, or guarantee a particular result.
science.limitationThree: It is general wellness information for adults, not a diagnosis or medical treatment.
science.limitationFour: For medical conditions, medication questions, pregnancy, or persistent sleep problems, consult a qualified health professional.
